speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I be permitted, first of all, to congratulate most sincerely the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. George) and the hon. member for Lake St. John (Mr. Gauthier) on the fluency with which they discharged their ever pleasant duties as mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I must say that I have been a member of federal or provincial legislatures for the past twenty-five years and that I have always admired the movers and seconders of the address. Providence did not give me that opportunity, but I feel no bitterness and I am happy to congratulate those who meet with as much success as those two members have had in the discharge of that duty.
Since the last session, Mr. Speaker, the association of free countries that make up the commonwealth has been bereaved by the passing of His Majesty King George VI.
The loss which was felt by the leaders of the free nations has been shared, not only
by the commonwealth countries but by the whole world.
I know that certain political thinkers do not believe in royalty, take it to be a somewhat obsolete institution handed down to us by the governments of the Middle Ages, and that the loss of a king leaves them rather indifferent. I believe that there is a place for good kings at the head of a country, that exemplary sovereigns like the one we have just lost are an inspiration for all forms of government to profit by, whether it be in the social, the family or the political sphere, so that all the laws enacted by these governments will tend to develop in the minds of their citizens the virtues of good citizenship, loyalty and respect of family ties, so as to counteract those dangerous modern concepts which tend to tear asunder family ties by refusing to endow them with the indispensable characteristics of strength and permanence.
The royal family has never, at any time or in any place, failed to provide us with an example of perfect unity. The royal family is undoubtedly the most valuable jewel which adorns the crown.
The passing of the head of the British empire has not weakened its ties. His successor, practically a mere child although she is a mother-the young queen, whose smile is still in the minds of our people as she seemed at times to give a questioning look to her prince charming, seeking advice or guidance-ascends the throne of England after having been brought up by a father and mother such as all countries must wish for.	i
While she was still a princess she already displayed, in a message to the mothers of the empire, great concern for sound family ties as she asked the mothers not to fail in the duties, the sorrows and the cares of motherhood. Through her example, she repeats the same message. She always keeps her smile and always holds the confidence of all mothers worthy of the name.
Not only is she a mother, she also takes upon herself another very heavy task and reigns over millions of people. Her own family is perfectly united; may God grant that the broader family of her subjects shall profit by the virtues and the affection which she has displayed.
If I have endeavoured to speak of the royal family it is because, like many others, I feel that the social cell of family is seriously menaced today and that the example thus set might give food for thought even to the

most apathetic minds; it might waken up all those who have been quite oblivious of the world in which they live; to those who advocate unlimited liberty at any cost, it might show the dangers awaiting them along the path on which they tread and even stop their descent on the down grade, and maybe lead them away from the slope along which they are sliding down faster and faster, carried away by the shallowness of their approach to the problems of the unity and permanence of family ties.
To proceed along that line, Mr. Speaker, would lead me to deal with a matter which has already been discussed in this house and which no doubt will come up again when the bill sponsored by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) is placed before us. I shall have more to say on that occasion.
At any rate, the world would be well-advised to follow the course set by the royal family, which has given us such a splendid example of solidarity, of unity and of all those civic virtues which are in such great need today. That example should be followed by all. It should be commented upon and brought to the attention of the most humble, especially those who have not much chance of listening to the radio or of reading newspapers and periodicals.
I wanted to mention that example, which should be a source of admiration to everyone. This is not only lip service on my part, but a sincere tribute.
I now wish to draw the attention of the house to another fact which, in my opinion, constitutes a rather serious problem for Canada. I want to say a word about the numerous human lives lost by fire. All those who, like myself, read newspapers and periodicals regularly-and we hear of those things mostly through the newspapers-must have noticed the large number of children who have lost their lives during the past two years in fires that have burnt down their homes. Their numbers moreover have been constantly on the increase.
There certainly is negligence somewhere, possibly thoughtlessness, possibly, too, a lack of knowledge of the operation of the newer heating appliances. In any event, every two or three days our dailies or weeklies report some fire which has killed one, two, three, four or five children and sometimes even the father and mother along with them. I think there is truly negligence somewhere.
13, 1952	403
The Address-Mr. P. Gauthier
I remember one case very well. Four children burned to death while the father and mother were absent; the house had been left in the care of a little twelve year old girl. To my mind, that is unforgiveable.
I am not suggesting that all deaths by fire are due to negligence of that kind, but it seems to me that our children are well worth the sacrifices the parents must make by giving up a few hours at the movies.
Those who use heating appliances do not go to the trouble of learning how to operate them. Certainly explosions in oil or gas stoves are much too frequent. You undoubtedly have noticed that there are more and more of these explosions every year.
In Canada and in the United States, we have what we call "fire prevention week". If fire prevention does, not come within the federal government's jurisdiction, it must come under some other authority. I therefore urge the governments of the provinces, of the larger cities and of the lesser municipalities to consider extending the period during which fire prevention is taught in order that all our citizens may be warned of the dangers present in their heating appliances. In that way, they would be made to understand that very young children should not be left in the care of a ten or twelve year old child because they could be burnt to death since the young guardian does not know enough and is certainly too young to run a house in the absence of the parents.
Fire prevention week should be observed throughout the country, even in the smallest parish, if we wish to put a stop to the enormous losses in human lives which we have suffered, especially in the past two years.
Mr. Speaker, it was my intention to raise here a question which concerns the hog producers of my constituency. I discussed this with the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and he supplied me with an answer. There is no doubt that the problem raises the question of federal and of provincial jurisdictions.
In any case, since the federal government has decided to purchase any surplus of hogs at 26 cents a pound, ordinary people believe, -and I do not blame them,-that the federal government has established a minimum price of 26 cents per pound.
As a result, hog raisers of my constituency, who were building up an interesting business in that field, have to sell their grade A and grade B-l hogs not at 25 or 26 cents per pound, but at 20, 18 and even 15 cents per pound, thereby losing large sums of money.

The Address-Mr. P. Gauthier They have sent a delegation to my office and submitted resolutions passed by municipal councils. They have asked me to see that something is done to remedy the situation. I am awaiting a reply from the Minister of Agriculture. If provincial governments that are jealously preserving their rights are going to do something to maintain the retail price of pork, I hope that they will give our farmers the help they need by providing them with the necessary protection so that they will not lose quite so much money. It so happens that the price of crushed feed has not gone down very much, not as far as I know, anyhow. They find that the costs of raising hogs are sufficiently high nowadays and that there is no need for the government to inflict upon them such a heavy loss by forcing them to sell their hogs at less than 26 cents and even as low as 15 cents a pound.
I now wish to speak of a matter which was brought up the other day by the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll). I do not see him in his seat just now but I know he is a very busy man. He spoke of this question with great frankness and courage. I wish to continue my remarks in English.
(Text):
I want to state as clearly as possible my position with respect to this question of immigration. I see the minister in his place.
I have full confidence in him, and I know he has competent officials working with him. I am sure he will understand the position I am taking toward this problem.
In stating my position I shall avail myself of the opportunity to place on record some quotations. In doing so I hope I shall not be breaking the rules of debate to too great an extent. I would ask your good will, Mr. Speaker, and the good will of hon. members so that I may be permitted to place these quotations on record.
When in 1950 I spoke in the house on this question I quoted the policy of the former prime minister, the Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King, a policy which I know is that of the present minister, and of the government as a whole. Speaking on May 1, 1947, as reported at page 2646 of Hansard, Mr. King said:
With regard to the selection of immigrants, much has been said about discrimination. I wish to make it quite clear that Canada is perfectly within her rights in selecting the persons whom we regard as desirable future citizens.
That is the position I take gladly now, and that I have taken in the past. He said further: There will, I am sure, be general agreement with the view that the people of Canada do not [Mr. Gauthier (Portneuf) .1
wish, as a result of mass immigration, to make a fundamental alteration in the character of our population.
In my view that is a sound and accurate statement, and sets forth what is to this day the policy of the government and of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Harris). If at this time I try to make my position clear, I do so because some people in other provinces seem to be under the impression that, generally speaking, the majority of people in Quebec are absolutely and radically opposed to immigration. I shall have some further quotations to make to prove that, on the contrary, they are not radically opposed to immigration, but that they want a very selective immigration.
Before making further observations, however, I shall quote the words of Miss Betty B. Robinson, M.A., who lectured at McMaster university in April of 1949 on the question of immigration. At that time she said this: It Is better to be overcautious than to be reckless in the matter of immigration.
These are strong and very accurate words. I should like to quote at the same time Mr. James S. Duncan, who has been quoted already by the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll), and who had this to say on the same occasion at McMaster university:
A thoroughly competent and adequate organization in the British Isles and Europe for screening, selecting and facilitating the movement to Canada of the best immigrant types-by all means let us screen and select those whom we desire among like-minded peoples.
I stress those words, because I wish to impress the house with the fact that I am in favour of a very thorough screening of all immigrants. I believe, further, that we cannot have a thorough screening if we support a policy of mass immigration. In the quotations I have read it will be clear to hon. members-and 1 refer to the quotations from the words of Miss Robinson and Mr. Duncan -that they always advocate a perfect screening and a good choice of immigrants. These statements are not made by French-Canadians from Quebec; rather they are made by English Canadians at McMaster university. I do not say this with any purpose of raising a racial issue; indeed, that would be far from my mind. I do it only to point out to hon. members that my native province is not so much opposed to immigration properly carried out, but that it is opposed to mass immigration.
I now turn to a quotation from La Terre de Chez Nous of June 13, 1950, where it says:
It is not enough to have fairer immigration regulations. They must also be put to good use. Immigrants from France have access to our country just like those from England and the United

States. Many French people wish to settle in Canada. This contribution from the mother country could be useful to us in a thousand ways.
Here, however, the provincial authorities or some private organization would have to be willing to take care of them. What has been done in this respect? Silence is the only answer.
The complaint is that no proper organization is doing anything for the immigrants to help them settle in Quebec. Reference is made to an inquiry conducted by Le Devoir in the following words:
One wonders, finally, If now we will see the province of Quebec admit French immigrants in as large a number as the group of British people welcomed to Ontario. Observers feel that it is up to Mr. Duplessis and the industrialists of this province.
If British immigrants settled in great numbers in the neighbouring province, it is due to the fact that, first of all, Premier Drew went and fetched them in Great Britain and that, with the agreement of Ontario employers, he opened a provincial employment bureau for immigrants in London.
I think we should do the same thing. There should be a Quebec provincial employment office in London, in France, in Belgium or in the Netherlands to select the immigrants we want and bring them to our province. I continue to quote:
If we want the French to settle here, our government and our businessmen should do likewise. If we feel that recent immigration from Britain disrupts the ethnical balance of our country, the remedy lies, after all, in our own hands.
Surely no one can take us to task when we try to preserve the ethnic balance between provinces. Surely no one can object if Quebec desires immigrants from Belgium, from Holland, from Italy and other countries the same as the other provinces want more British immigrants. We simply want to maintain the ethnic balance between the different provinces of Canada. We accept British immigrants in Quebec and we get along quite happily with them. If anyone wants to see how we get along all he needs to do is to visit our province and see how we treat our minority.
Surely the way I am speaking does not indicate that I want to raise a racial issue in connection with immigration. That is the farthest from my mind. I simply want to state our position as clearly as possible. We are ready to accommodate selected immigrants, but we do not want to take a chance on what has happened in the past happening in the future. As the hon. member for Spadina (Hr. Croll) said the other day, people have come to this country with the promise to be good citizens but they have turned around and stabbed us in the back. We want law-abiding citizens; we want good settlers; we want good farmers.
The Address-Mr. P. Gauthier
I should like to refer to Relations of January 1950, a periodical issued by the Jesuit fathers. They quote Maclean's magazine as follows:
According to Premier Frost, the population of Ontario increases by 10,000 people a month and now exceeds four and a half million. The largest of our provinces keeps its lead: Quebec has less than 4 million people and its population increases by only 8,000 a month.
One reason why the people in Quebec were not in favour of immigration in the past is that we always trusted in Providence, we always had enough children to fill up our empty spaces, provide the necessary hands to do our agricultural work and help in the development of the wealth of our province. But the way things have been going, Quebec will have to do something about immigration. I have often been quoted as being one who was almost radically opposed to immigration, but I have had to change my mind because of conditions we have had to meet after the war, especially in connection with displaced persons. I shall continue with this quotation from Maclean's magazine as follows:
Autonomy allows others, smarter than we, to bring in reinforcements, tens of thousands of refugees, especially British or Dutch, who are well established on farms. The Pope has asked countries with vast territories to receive those who have none left, since that is better than almsgiving. Will Quebec therefore continually refuse to open its doors, its barricaded territories, even to our own kin?
Le Canada of June 13, 1950, had this to say:
The era of mass immigration to Canada has come to an end because the conditions that inspired it are no longer in force . . . but from the simple point of humanitarianism we cannot close our doors to foreigners who seek to establish themselves here. This does not mean we should accept anybody whatsoever, but we should exercise a judicious choice. Nor is the question of offering a welcome to these new Canadians something we should longer neglect. It is our duty to initiate them into the way Canadians live and to facilitate their assimilation. The new minister of immigration has a full enough program facing him and he will be able doubtlessly to rise to the heights of his task.
I think the minister has risen to his task. I think he has done a good gob. I shall come back to this a little later. I have received complaints from some of my municipalities, sometimes in the form of resolutions, asking me to contact different industries to ask them not to take immigrants in the place of nationals who may have been living for generations in the vicinity of their factory. I have contacted these officials and while I must admit that in a few cases immigrants have been hired, the fact is that to a great extent our nationals have had the preference in these industries. I was speaking to one of the officials of the department of immigration last night on the telephone and he told

The Address-Mr. P. Gauthier me that all the immigrants who had been gathered at St. Paul l'Ermite, the immigration station at Quebec, were being placed in other industries and it was being found that the task was not too hard.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at six o'clock I was continuing my expose of opinions expressed by certain newspapers and periodicals in the province of Quebec. I have here a few words in French by Eugene L'Heureux, under date of Monday, March 10, 1952:
(Translation):
. . . Pope Pius XII, on several occasions since the war, has requested the thinly populated countries to receive charitably the families and individuals who are compelled to leave their country because of these extremely difficult times.
And Mr. L'Heureux writes further:
Nevertheless, immigration is necessary at this time. People call it a necessary evil or an appreciable blessing, according to their degree of optimism and their capacity for gauging future requirements for the accomplishment of difficult tasks.
And Mr. L'Heureux quotes Le Droit thus:
The editor of Le Droit of Ottawa was right when he wrote:	From all that has been written in the
newspapers for some time and from what we have been able to learn from the immigrants themselves, it is clear that immigration must be organized

methodically in the province of Quebec if that province is to profit by it. That systematic planning requires the co-operation of the government and of the main public bodies in a provincial organization.
(Text):
I think Le Soleil was right in saying this:
It is impossible to oppose all immigration in principle, provided that it be reasonable, in good order, well selected and in no way directed against one of the two principal elements of the Canadian population. This is what our representatives in the commons must say when the opportunity arises, and they must demand a guarantee that immigration must be kept within fair limits if recruiting begins again.
Then L'Action Catholique, another French newspaper in the Quebec district, was quoted by The Ensign in August, 1950, as follows:
French Canadians know that, on the slightest economic set-back, the province of Quebec is always hit harder than others, that the number of unemployed is more considerable and that unemployment lasts longer. Without rejecting the different alleged explanations of this unfavourable situation: they persist in believing that the fundamental reason rests on an excess population of which they should dispose.
They do not agree that they should1 eliminate this excess population by the artificial and immoral means of birth control. They believe that the country should make the necessary provisions to establish this surplus population, make use of the new generations by opening new centres and employing arable lands. They believe that the appropriation of these natural endowments and land should first be made by the sons of Canada.
With these reservations they do not oppose the admission into the country of a number of immigrants proportionate to the capacity of absorption of the Canadian population.
And The Ensign adds:
The firm stand of L'Action Catholique supported The Ensign view that "immigration has never, nor will it ever, be a substitute for natural growth."
Of course in the province of Quebec we always have confidence that the natural growth of our families will make provision for filling the empty spaces and for the work force necessary to make our natural resources more productive. The other day the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) had this to say at page 290 of Hansard:
Today a nation more than twice as large in population as it was in 1913, and many times as strong, is taking in only half the number of immigrants we took in at that time. I merely point out to the house that it is time we burst these bonds of caution.
I think these are very strong words from the mouth of a usually cool-tempered, man such as the hon. member for Spadina. We will never be too cautious. I imagine that past years have taught us greater care, and I cannot imagine that the necessary screening would remain fully efficient if all we said and did was "Bring them in". It is true that we received twice as many immigrants in 1913, but what was our population then? It was half what it is today. The more our

population grows the less space we have, and the longer it takes to absorb them or at least find them shelter, food and employment. I do not agree with the hon. member for Spadina when he says our immigrants do not have to be absorbed, that they only have to be placed. I think the first thing we must do is look upon the immigrants as people who in one way or another must be absorbed so as to become good citizens, rather than as people just coming here for homes and jobs.
It is all very well and easy to select those who want to leave their country in quest of a better future, but to be honest we must tell them the exact situation. During the last number of months we have heard many complaints from immigrants. Some go so far as to say they have been lured by the promised facilities they would find here, the big money they would earn, the jobs waiting for them and so on. We have to be careful; and we must not be surprised if many try their chances over the border. The question of our ability to absorb must never be overlooked. Then at page 291 of Hansard the hon. member had this to say:
From 1945 to 1950 Canada admitted 568,000 immigrants, an average of 95,000 a year . . . During that same period 314.600 persons left Canada, by the back door I think, to go to the United States or other places.
I have seen in some newspapers that the number of people migrating from one country to another, especially from Canada to the United States, is around 25,000 a year. If we take that figure from the 314,000, to be conservative, we have the approximate figure of our loss. A good part of what is left represents immigrants. Do you not see that the question of absorption comes into the picture once more? Then why spend the public money to send immigrants to the United States, when that country is as wealthy as we are? I repeat that our ability to absorb decreases in direct ratio to the increase of our population. Again at page 290 the hon. member said that Alberta had an increase of 17-6 per cent. Of course for the last five or six years the oil industry in that province has been attracting many of our own nationals as well as many immigrants. Next to Alberta is Saskatchewan with a loss of 7-5 per cent. Well, I ask myself where these people have gone from Saskatchewan. No doubt some have gone to Alberta, some to British Columbia, and some to the United States. Many have left farms, and those farms have been either taken up by other farmers or left uncultivated. We know that in the west today, especially in Saskatchewan and Manitoba, we need new farmers.
The figures given by the member for Spadina (Mr. Croll), which I quoted this
The Address-Mr. P. Gauthier afternoon, show that only 25,000 out of 194,000 immigrants who entered the country in 1951 were farmers. Only 25,000 were farmers, but we need about 200,000 farmers. Certainly half our immigrants should be farmers, because there are many areas in this country which need to be cultivated. I feel that we should take special care to bring to this country as many farmhands as we can, rather than bring people who are not qualified specialists. I believe the hon. member for Spadina showed that over 35,000 of the immigrants were unskilled labourers. Certainly those people are not going on the farms, they are going into the cities. I hope that we shall not have another economic depression like the one we had between 1930 and 1935. If we do, we shall see the breadlines again.
I do not agree with the member for Spadina, Mr. Speaker, when he says that in 1940 we did not have the labour necessary to perform our duty and help our allies win the war. We certainly would not have amazed Mr. Churchill if there had been any such lack of employees during 1940-45. The hon. member mentioned the attitude of labour towards immigration. I have here a copy of a lecture given by Professor H. A. Logan, Ph. D., of the department of political economy, university of Toronto. He had this to say about the attitude of labour towards immigration:
For labour's attitudes toward immigration we look mainly to the expressions of the labour congresses. Judged by this source, the voice of labour has been consistently, until the end of the war, a protest voice. The Trades and Labour Congress (TLC) from its beginning in the eighties, like the American Federation of Labour (AFL) in the United States, has stood for restriction, especially of urban worker types, who are seen as a threat to the standards of living by its own members. Across the years it has expressed the views of the building trades, railway unions, printers and metal trades. In depressions, it has twice advocated complete temporary prohibition.
With the social laws passed by this government, we shall not witness a depression of the kind we witnessed between 1930 and 1935. I have to say that in praise of the government, and I thank the government for those laws. I know that the people are grateful for these social measures, and according to Professor Logan the same attitude is taken by the labour congresses. I continue to quote from Professor Logan:
Specifically, at all times, the TLC has condemned "irresponsible" advertising and "misrepresentation" by railways, employers' associations, private employment exchanges, and steamship companies, and of all who may be interested in immigration for profit; opposed passage, when assisted financially by dominion and provincial governments and charitable societies; also "contract labour" brought

The Address-Mr. A. Stewart
in directly by particular employers (qualified recently by the clause "unless certified as necessary by national employment service").
During the war that was the policy adopted by these labour organizations. I have not the quotation here, but I am sure that somewhere I have seen that during the war the labour organizations asked for selective immigration. They want qualified men to come here, and ask that our economy be not disrupted by permitting too many immigrants to enter the country.
I believe I have made my position quite clear, Mr. Speaker, on the question of immigration. I have quoted many periodicals from my province, and I think I have expressed the opinion of the majority of the people of Quebec. This afternoon I said that I felt it was natural that the English-speaking provinces preferred immigrants from British sources, but they also receive immigrants from all countries in Europe. I recall that in 1950 one member of the Conservative party said he had Italian immigrants working for him. This afternoon I asked him if he was still satisfied with the Italian immigrants, and he said they were still working for him and doing a good job. In some provinces there are immigrants from Latvia, from Poland and from other countries in Europe.
I believe the people of my province are satisfied with the work these immigrants are doing on their farms. I come back to this, though, that the contract the immigrant signs with the department is for too short a period1. It should be for more than one year-and here I am addressing the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg)-in order to give these immigrants an opportunity of understanding the people for whom they are working and understanding our way of life. It would enable these people to understand and to like their surroundings in Quebec, and might induce them to settle in our province. These immigrants are good people who are trying to give satisfaction and live up to their pledge.
I think -my position is clear. I do not have to add anything, but I shall repeat this advice given by Miss Betty B. Robinson which I quoted this afternoon:
It is better to be overcautious than to be reckless in the matter of immigration.
I do not oast blame on anyone, but I think 100,000 immigrants in a year are as many as Canada can possibly absorb.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I intend to answer the speech made this afternoon by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson). I intend to show and to prove that the statement issued by the national council of the C.C.F. was
[Mr. Gauthier (Portneuf) .1
factually correct and also correct in its implications. I intend to prove that the statement issued by NATO that we shall provide approximately fifty divisions in appropriate conditions of combat readiness this year is impossible of achievement, and therefore irresponsible.
Before I go on with that, there is a matter which I must bring up, and which is not at all apart from the subject of national defence. On several occasions during this session I have spoken in the house about the situation of packing house workers throughout Canada due to the most expensive mistake ever perpetrated by any department of the government. Several hundreds are unemployed due to foot-and-mouth disease. Plants have been closed in Regina. When I asked the ministers of the crown what the intentions of the government were in the way of recompensing these men, I was told that they would get unemployment insurance

after, of course, they had waited nine days. Now, owing to provincial action, packing house workers in other provinces are becoming unemployed. But when I asked the government what its policy was, I was not told the whole story; for apparently if the government did not have a policy, at least the Department of National Defence did. When this house approved unanimously last year the goal of 115,000 troops for our defence, some of us felt that that number could only be recruited to some extent by economic compulsion; and that indeed is what is happening today, for the Department of National Defence, through the army recruiting office in Winnipeg, is explicitly directing advertisements in these terms:
Packing House Workers
Do you want a pay cheque this month?
That is a nice question to ask those who are unemployed.
Men are being accepted daily at new higher rates of pay, with no lay-offs and no loss of pay through illness or injury. Men accepted are assured of steady employment . . .

I am convinced-and I have said this frequently- that the rulers of the Kremlin believe that war between Russia and the west is inevitable but not necessarily today or not necessarily this year. As a democratic socialist I know something about communism, and I despise it; so we in the C.C.F. cannot in good conscience be partners to any policy which we believe will play into the hands of those in the Kremlin. Hence, when we see policies which we believe do so, we state our opposition in this house.
It might be said that there is little room indeed for a meeting of the minds between Russians and ourselves. But even if the room for it is only the size of a pinhead we have to continue to do as we as a nation have been doing in the past; that is we have to try to arrive at some modus vivendi between the two conflicting camps. Otherwise the alternative is war; and nobody in his sane senses should ask once again that the dark ingenuity of science should ravish the face of this earth, that Europe should become a shambles, that millions of innocent people should be killed. Although we win the war we in North America would still be the losers.
War we do not want if we can possibly and honourably avoid it, and so we have to try to arrive at a modus vivendi with Russia. But I and my colleagues are convinced that we can only do so from a position of strength, and that position of strength in Europe today is the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, and we do not want to see it imperilled by policies which we believe are wrong.
In his broadcast the other night the minister said that the communists believe that NATO is an aggressive organization and they say that NATO is an aggressive military alliance.
We disagree with them. The minister then went on to say: It is sad to see that the C.C.F. seem to be moving towards this position.
If anybody says that they see anything of the sort then they suffer from myopic astigmatism. We are very far removed indeed from that position. The minister then goes on to quote from the statement of the C.C.F. council:
NATO policies seem to have fallen under the control of the military.
Well, let us examine this statement. I hold in my hand an excerpt from a quite responsible magazine, the United States News and World Report of last July. What I have is an article by Robert Kleiman, who is European regional editor of that paper. He had been at SHAPE and had seen how NATO was working, and this is what he said then:
A new strategic concept of what it takes to defend Europe is one key to Eisenhower's assurance in the face of difficulties. He has decided that the Atlantic pact will be a success if he can


get 20 to 25 combat-ready divisions backed by adequate air power into line in Europe by next summer.
The new objective replaces the theory that nothing less than 60 to 100 divisions can make Europe secure.
I quote that to show that in Eisenhower's headquarters last summer they believed that 20 to 25 divisions this summer would be adequate. I have here-and I am calling others to witness rather than make these statements on my own-a statement of Walter Kerr, a correspondent of New York Herald Tribune. On the 20th of October last, writing from Paris, he says:
... it might be possible to approach the goal fixed by the military experts: about fifty active divisions by July 1 1954 and another fifty more reserve divisions . . .
The Toronto Globe and Mail on December 17 last published a dispatch to the effect that Eisenhower was asking for forty divisions by the end of 1952 and sixty divisions or more by 1954; and yet we are presented with this document which states fifty divisions at the end of this year. Am I to be told that the civilian heads of governments who were at Lisbon insisted that the military should raise their sights to fifty divisions? If that has happened then a revolution has come about. I have never known an example of where military men had to be induced to raise their sights, but on the contrary I am confident that in every case they have had to diminish them. Therefore when I say that we in the C.C.F. agree that when this was done it was because of military pressure, there is ample evidence to show it.
In his speech this afternoon the minister said that we supported higher figures last year. What were the figures which were given us last year? They were figures which the minister himself knew, figures apparently much higher than fifty divisions for this year, yet nobody else knew them. But it is very dangerous indeed when Canada is placed in the position where hidden commitments are made and the people of Canada know nothing about them. I am not disputing the minister's words that commitments were higher a year ago, but I do say that it is dangerous to have those high commitments, terribly dangerous, and not to let parliament know about them.
What is the situation now? I hear somebody who wishes to ask a question.

Here again I have before me a document- and I cannot vouch for its authenticity, because the original is marked "confidential" and I have not seen it. However it is a report of a committee of the North Atlantic community which dealt with political, economic, social and cultural fields, and of which our own Secretary of State for External Affairs was chairman. I am informed that the first section of this report dealt with closer consultation among the NATO powers, particularly with a view to preventing a recurrence of happenings such as the United States suddenly deciding that Germany must be rearmed, or that Greece and Turkey must come into the North Atlantic treaty alliance.
As I say, it is right and salutary that we should be prepared to expostulate and to object, upon occasions. That does not mean in any way that we do not recognize what the American people have done for freedom in this world, or the magnitude of the sacrifice they have made. But it does not mean we are thereby prepared to be gagged because of that same American generosity. That is realized and recognized even in the United States. In this connection I quote the statement of Clarence Decker, mutual

.security agency assistant director in the Far East. Mr. Decker had this to say on February 26 of this year:
The United States must learn that its concept of freedom is not the only one which is opposed to tyranny. He questioned the wisdom of foreign economic aid predicated on agreements by recipient governments to follow any future United States course of action.
And because some of these offers of aid were predicated upon supporting American policy, ten nations, so far as I know, have refused it in this form. On the other hand you have this extraordinarily generous manifestation which took place in New Delhi a few weeks back when Mr. Chester Bowles, American Ambassador to India, gave freely, and without any strings attached, $50 million to the Indian people from Americans so that they could help themselves. If we or the United States wish to make friends and influence people then we should give for the sake of giving, we should help for the sake of helping. If we put strings or ties on what we give, then instead of making friends we shall indeed be incurring enemies.
We are not anti-American any more than we are anti-NATO. What we are against is deluding, not only the people of this country but the people of other countries as to what NATO actually is doing. We say that fifty divisions are impossible. The minister agrees that there may not be fifty divisions. I said earlier that Mr. Lovett, secretary of defence of the United States, said the same thing. Mr. Lovett described as a very powerful force the more than 25 combat divisions and 20 plus ready reserve divisions pledged by signatories to the 14-nation pact during the coming year.
That is a vastly different statement from that which was made in the NATO release, vastly different indeed. Mr. Reston of the New York Times said so later, and I quote:
-they agreed in Lisbon to do these things:

What was that propaganda eye on? We submit that that eye was on the United States election. The minister has done likewise in every speech he has made since he has come to this house. Yet what has been the measure of our aid during the last five years? It has amounted to less than the cost of one package of cigarettes per capita of the
The Address-Mr. A. Stewart Canadian people per annum-$25 million for the Colombo plan. The Secretary of State for External Affairs has stated that we have to give economic aid, and he is right, but the government has voted against the possibility of economic aid.
It was hoped to set up an international development authority in the United Nations which would have the power to make grants and loans to underdeveloped countries. What did Canada do? Our Secretary of State for External Affairs has said that we should support this, but Canada, through the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson), opposes it.
We have a situation where the nations of Europe are asking us for vital raw materials. It would be a far better thing for us to give these European nations raw materials out of which they can make the arms that they need; it would be a far better thing for us in the long run to help Europe to build itself up so that it can produce these arms; but what is our answer when they come to us and ask for aid in the form of raw materials-it is "undesirable in principle".
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) cannot agree he says, because we have a dollar imbalance in trade. If we were serious in this we could find that $100 million and it would pay us tenfold.
That is a sort of help we should be giving, but we refuse to give it. On the other hand, while we permit those who are wealthy to spend their winters in Florida we insist on the packing house workers being conscripted into the army. There is not much equity there, nor is there much justice. Our position has been-this is the position which I have stated in my own constituency, to the people to whom I am directly responsible-that the best and shortest way of combating communism is by providing economic aid. I am convinced that if it is necessary to increase taxes in order to supply economic aid to Europe to enable those countries to combat communism, the people whom I represent would be quite prepared to accept those increased taxes. So would most others.

Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to deal with any of the particular phases of this debate which have been developed in recent hours, but there are some observations I should like to make which, although general, I feel are fundamental and of basic importance to us as a nation.
Since I last rose to speak in this house the whole western world was shocked to hear of the sudden and untimely death of our late King George VI. But in our sorrow we were comforted by the knowledge that the monarchy, like life itself, has continuity and stability, a continuity which does not stem from any individual but simply from the fact that when one generation has run its course there is another to take up the torch in its place. I think I speak for every member of this house when I say that our sympathy is with our young Queen in the task 

which destiny has called her to take up at this time.
That leads me to make this observation. There is a belief that when a queen rules over us it is an age of great hope, when we can look for a better standard of living, a greater measure of self-respect and prestige in the world, and a time of general prosperity. In the case of two queens especially, Queen Elizabeth I and Queen Victoria, history bears out that belief. I think perhaps it would not be amiss to look back and see what were the characteristics which marked the men in places of responsibility in those ages. If we do so I think we will find that men in responsible positions in those two golden ages had the characteristics of industry and enterprise. They were ready and quick to defend their rights, their liberties and themselves against all comers. They had faith in themselves, yet coupled with that faith they had a deep humility, recognizing that while considerable power might have been given them as individuals, nevertheless they were very small cogs in the general scheme of things.
Those people, with those characteristics, received certain rewards which the whole of mankind thirsts for in this very day. They were rewarded by great discoveries, both geographic and scientific. There were rewards of material gain. In those circumstances the standard of living of our people rose very considerably. There were great advances in the arts, letters and sciences, and there was a tremendous advance in world prestige. The people had a satisfactory sense of purpose in their lives and I maintain that these are the very rewards all mankind is searching for today.
It might not be amiss to assume that if these are the rewards we seek, the characteristics which brought them about in the past might also bring them at the present time. We as a nation are wandering hither and yon with no definite sense of purpose and no discernible goal. Those of us who have travelled in England will know that there is a great irregularity about the countryside, and it is very easy to become lost and confused. You imagine there is no order about anything, no sense of direction and no straight line leading anywhere. But if you fly over England you can plainly discern the old Roman roads radiating in every direction, joining the old Roman towns of England. In the same way, if we can raise ourselves above the petty jealousies of local viewpoints and prejudices of various kinds, and as a nation try to see what our goal should be, at least we will find various roads open to us and will be in a position to select the goal for which we as a nation should strive.

These times, therefore, require a standard of statesmanship which is not often evident in this country. It requires a type of leadership which will give us purpose as a nation, and which will indicate to the whole western world that Canada is prepared to give leadership to that world where it has obligations in that regard. On many occasions this government, instead of that type of statesmanship, has shown a desire to trim its sails to every fickle wind of public fancy that happens to blow. They explain, of course, that they are a middle-of-the-road party, that they believe in certain principles of compromise, and that being a middle-of-the-road party they do not expect to satisfy everyone or even a large number of people but they hope to almost satisfy a majority. They preach certain principles of compromise, but I am afraid that on some occasions at least they practise the compromise of certain principles. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, one of our greatest Canadian statesmen, on one occasion said the twentieth century belonged to Canada. If he were alive today I think he would be disillusioned and disheartened because of the way we as a country have wandered hither and yon, making only vague and general progress toward our goal.
When one travels over western Europe, through northern France and the low countries, one observes that the roads are crooked and winding, and seemingly without very much direction. Suddenly, when you are still some distance from your destination, you notice that the road becomes perfectly straight, and quite frequently dead ahead in the middle of the road is the spire of the cathedral of the next town. That is not so by chance. It is so because the pilgrims of the middle ages in making their progress in a vague and wandering fashion toward their destination would eventually come to the brow of a hill from which they could see the spire of the cathedral ahead. Then they made a beeline for it. The travellers through the centuries have followed in that way, and the roads have grown up in that fashion.
So it is today. We need courage, we need integrity and we need enterprise. We need in this country a goal that all Canadians, regardless of racial origin, religious beliefs or vocation, can work and progress toward with energy and satisfaction and unity. If this country has a government with the courage and energy to demonstrate these characteristics, then, as in the Elizabethan period, the era which this rich young country is now entering will be truly a golden age.

Mr. Speaker, we are now going to hear French spoken for at least a quarter of an hour; our English-speaking friends on both sides of the house, many of whom understand the beautiful French language, are those who often rejoice most in hearing French spoken here; for them, I shall endeavour to speak as distinctly as I can.
I want to take advantage of this debate to submit two recommendations to the government, concerning the improvement of telephone communications in Quebec's rural districts and more particularly in Bonaventure county, which I represent. It is an urgent problem, for about 80 per cent of the farmhouses in the province of Quebec are still without telephones.
On December 31, 1948, there were, in our province, 49,083 rural residential telephones. But the 1941 census showed that there were 217,308 rural homes. It is therefore evident that scarcely 22 out of each 100 farms are telephone subscribers in the province of Quebec. The province of Ontario is much more privileged from that standpoint and has made much more progress than the province of Quebec in that sphere. According to statistics there are, in that province, 150,371 telephones for 351,770 rural establishments, or 41.4 apparatus per 100 farms, compared to 22 in the province of Quebec.
Moreover, while urban telephone systems are being modernized by the installation of automatic devices, the few telephones to be found on the farms are of am obsolete type, manually operated and branched in groups of 10, 15 or even 20 on the same circuit.
Yet our farmers, and more particularly those who live far from villages, deserve a better telephone service than they are now getting. The telephone is an essential means of communication for the farmer. It is absolutely necessary in cases of emergency, such as when sickness strikes his family or his herd.
While an increasing number of farmers are asking for a decent telephone service in their homes, the telephone companies of the province seem incapable of extending their lines throughout rural districts in order that this service may be within reach of all those farmers who are asking for it.
One of the main reasons why our people have been leaving the country has been the lack of those modern conveniences which the city dweller enjoys, such as electricity and telephone service.

The Address-Mr Arsenault
And yet, in the past ten years, the price of materials and labour in the telephone industry has more than doubled. As far as urban services were concerned, the telephone companies met this situation by increasing the efficiency of their system through the addition of new phones and the installation of more modern equipment, as well as through an increase in rates.
As far as rural phone service is concerned, the construction and operating costs have increased in like proportion. And yet it is almost impossible, with very few exceptions, to increase efficiency by adding new customers.
The number of farms per single range mile is 8 and in order to give adequate service, you necessarily have to lay one line for every 10 subscribers from the telephone central. On the other hand, a rural telephone service, whether it be a company or a syndicate, must have a return of 6 to 7 per cent on its invested capital, otherwise it cannot get the funds necessary for the operation and development of the service.
Only one telephone company in Quebec can afford to operate certain rural lines at a loss. That is the Bell Telephone Company, which serves all the large urban centres. Operating profits there will always cover deficits incurred by rural lines. This company owned, as at December 31, 1948, 20,212 rural residential telephones in Quebec out of a total of 519,319 telephones, or hardly 3 [DOT] 9 per cent.
But there are-I think this house will be surprised to hear-255 other telephone systems in the province of Quebec and their financial standing does not allow them to follow the policy of the Bell Telephone Company. The only way out for these 255 telephone systems is to double the present rural rates by bringing them, for example, to $5 per month, whereas they average now $2.50-and the number of rural customers of the systems would then fall materially-or to get financial aid from the government. The government, or the state, should not take the place of private enterprise, but it is the duty of the state to help private enterprise do its job.
In the United States, congress has solved this problem of rural telephones, after protracted research and numerous discussions, by reducing the cost of that service through financial aid from the government, in the form of loans to private enterprise at 2 per cent over a period of thirty-five years. The difference between the interest charged for
[Mr. Arsenault.!
those loans and their cost to the government is made up of taxes paid by the great telephone systems serving the large urban centres. In this way, Mr. Speaker, the subscribers in the large cities served by important companies pay for part of the service cost to the subscribers of smaller companies operating in rural areas.
One of the essential characteristics of the American policy is that the loans do not cover only the building of new rural lines, but also improvements to existing systems in the urban section of the exchanges concerned.
I fail to see, at least under the present circumstances, any other complete solution to the acute problem of rural telephones in the province of Quebec. Again I say it is not a case of the state or the government replacing private enterprise but of helping it to accomplish a task it is not capable of doing by its own means. Our agricultural economy would thus be improved. I respectfully ask the government, and in particular the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier), who has authority in the field of telegraph and telephone services, to study the problem very seriously in order to find a solution.
My second suggestion to the government is to increase, in the estimates, the amounts earmarked for repairing and extending telephone lines in settlements and other areas so remote from the main centres that private companies deem it economically impossible to extend their lines that far.
In the constituency of Bonaventure alone, 22 localities are almost without any telephone service.

On the contrary I believe these are first-class investments for a country like ours. It is, so to speak, charity on an international plane. I will go further and will say that I hope to see the day when all the countries in the world will have reached such a degree of civilization that at least half of the fabulous amounts now being spent on rearmament will be spent instead to help in the rehabilitation of resourceless countries or countries whose natural resources, during past centuries, have been sacrificed on the altar of imperialism.
We have a duty of justice and charity to fulfil in that respect and I know that the present government will not fail in this highly deserving task.
But the fact nevertheless remains that in our own country, with a wealth of the most diverse natural resources, there are thousands of our fellow Canadians who are unhappy because they do not have at their disposal means of communication considered essential like the telephone. We are not asking for millions. We are not from the West; we are from the East. A few thousand dollars more in the estimates of the Department of Transport under the item of telegraph and telephone would not make much difference but would render such a great service to our own people, particularly to those who have the courage to live in remote settlements or far from villages, towns or large centres, deprived of most of public services which are considered, at least in this century, as essential and indispensable, and of which the poorest workers in our large cities may avail themselves.
