subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire this evening to deal briefly
with one specific matter, namely Canada's housing shortage. Even today I find it hard to believe that this critical matter was not even mentioned in the speech from the throne. After all, in view of the proportions of the shortage, I think most Canadians were entitled to expect their government, in that speech, to at least show some interest in the subject, to mention it, or perhaps even to suggest some solution. Instead, in the throne speech this problem was completely ignored. It was treated with silence and apparently with indifference.
How serious is the housing shortage in Canada today? I think most members would have to admit that there are at least 650,000 Canadians who lack adequate housing. Heavier immigration, natural population increase and defence industries have all helped to aggravate the situation, particularly in recent years. Today thousands and thousands of Canadians are living in basements. Countless others are living in attics. Many families are living in one room, and some Canadians are even living in garages. I suggest that the conditions in which these people are living should arouse in this house indignation. Moreover, Mr. Speaker, the demand for housing is such that the situation seems to be becoming more serious with each successive week.
Last year I believe we brought to this country in the neighbourhood of 175,000 immigrants. I think the minister hopes to bring here roughly the same number in 1952. Every single week that goes by, thousands of new Canadians are coming to Canada. I congratulate the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Harris) on the success of his program; but I regret that the Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Winters) has not shown the same vigour and the same imagination in getting homes for these people. It seems to me that unless, at this session, parliament succeeds in getting some kind of an adequate house-building program under way, there is a danger that our immigration program will break down. After all, you cannot continue to bring in people indefinitely without having some place for them to live. I say that the demand for housing today is at an all-time high in Canada's history.
What about the supply of new houses? The supply situation could be summed up fairly well in this way in most communities. All housing is short. Rental housing is much shorter. Low-rental housing and low-cost housing are virtually non-existent across the nation. Today three-quarters of our population is not in a financial position to buy a new home. I am going to suggest tonight to this house that the supply situation, instead

The Address-Mr. Thatcher of improving, is month by month deteriorating. In the first eleven months of 1951, according to the dominion bureau of statistics, 25 per cent fewer houses were started than in the first eleven months of 1950. And what is even more significant, the trend in the later months is even more serious. In September of 1951 46 per cent fewer houses were started than in September of 1950. In October the drop was 49 per cent; and in November 1951, 43 per cent fewer houses were built than in November, 1950. Surely these figures and these building trends should cause some concern to parliament. I respectfully suggest that the time has come for us to analyse the reasons why, after seven years of peace, or relative peace, Canada's housing backlog, instead of improving, is becoming greater.
Is our shortage of housing caused by a shortage of materials? Such a shortage may be a factor, but I do not think it is a major factor. Certainly I can tell the house that in most hardware lines which are required for building there is no shortage; there are plenty of nails, plenty of lock sets, plenty of building paper, etc. As a matter of fact, during the past year most merchants have been plagued with inventories which were too high, rather than too low. I have talked to many lumber men who tell the same story. Possibly cement is a little short, and a few steel items, but by and large I am sure that the paucity of new houses is not caused primarily by a shortage of materials. But even if such were the case, I believe the minister would have the responsibility of giving to housing the necessary priority that it required to get essential materials. Perhaps I am biased but, as I see this problem, the main reason why houses are not being built more rapidly in Canada today is the almost insurmountable difficulty which Canadians meet when they try to finance their housing contracts.
The main responsibility for that fact must lie on the doorstep of the federal government. For instance, look at the down payment. Except for defence workers, since last February, 1951, a minimum down payment of 20 per cent has been required. In actual fact, for various technical reasons, the down payment is closer to 25 per cent. That means that a man needs at least $3,000 to build even a small house. You could build a whole house for that figure about ten years ago. Of course the result is that many people in the lower income groups simply cannot build. Surely then it would be a sensible step for parliament to take, if it wishes to get an adequate program under way, to drop the down payment requirements from 20 per cent to 10 per cent or less. I say that if


people in this country could build a house with $1,000 down, you would see mass production get started in a hurry.
But such action to be effective should be accompanied by a second step, namely, more extensive terms on the unpaid balance. The house will recall that when the National Housing Act was originally introduced it was hoped and expected that the insurance companies of this country, or perhaps I should say the lending institutions, would jointly finance most of the unpaid balance on these housing contracts over a 20-year period. For several years that method of financing was fairly successful. But recently, and particularly in the past twelve months, the insurance companies of this nation have been increasingly reluctant to lend money for house construction. As a matter of fact, I think there is in Canada today what might be called a semi-strike on the part of insurance companies against such lending.
In some parts of the country they are refusing to lend money for housing under any circumstances. In some of the more select areas such as Toronto, Montreal, Ottawa, Vancouver and a few other cities, they are still lending money, but they are lending it on very stringent terms. In other words, they are making a 50 per cent loan or a 70 per cent loan, which in effect means today that Canadians, far from having a 20 per cent down payment, are often having to pay anywhere from 30 per cent to 50 per cent down in hard cash before they can get a house started.
Why have the insurance companies or the lending institutions curtailed their loans for housing? I have heard several reasons suggested since I came to Ottawa last week. The first reason put forward is that interest rates are too low. If that is so, I suppose it is a fairly legitimate reason. If the insurance companies can lend money more profitably and more safely elsewhere I suppose we cannot blame them. Some might suggest that the interest return under N.H.A. should be increased by the government to these lending institutions. I for one do not believe that this would be a solution. The minister made such a move a short time ago, by raising the interest rate a half of one per cent. I think the insurance companies now get 5J per cent. The step at that time, however, did not have much effect, and there was not a great deal more money put into housing by the insurance companies. I think the danger is that if the interest rate gets too high, the cost to the house purchaser will become prohibitive.
There is another rumour which I have heard in the corridors of parliament, a rumour which I must say in fairness I can

hardly believe, though it has come to my ears on three or four occasions. It has been suggested that the insurance companies are engaging in this sit-down strike on house loans in order to pressure parliament into refraining from passing the annuities bill which is shortly to come before us. As I say, I cannot believe that this rumour is correct, and I certainly hope that it is not. Such pressure would be most ill-advised. But whatever the reasons are, the hard fact remains that the insurance companies in Canada today are not lending the money which is required by house builders to put up sufficient new houses. I say that unless the minister or someone can find some way of persuading the insurance companies to put up more money, some other method of financing will have to be found and found soon.
I say, Mr. Speaker, that at this moment there is legislation on the statute books to deal with just such a contingency. Some time ago parliament passed section 31A as an amendment to the National Housing Act. Under that section the minister is empowered through Central Mortgage, where the regular lending channels do not function, to lend money directly. But for one reason or another so far he has not seen fit to utilize that section to' any degree.
On Monday last, at page 250 of Hansard I asked the Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Winters) a direct question as follows:
Can people in cities over 5,000 who cannot get housing loans from insurance companies get them now from the government under section 31A of the act?
The minister's reply was most evasive. He did not answer yes and he did not answer no; but he did say-and again I quote:
I hope that the lending institutions will continue to play their traditional role in this field.
Well, I hope that they will also, but what if they don't? Today they are not playing their traditional role in so far as lending for housing is concerned. Where do we go now?
A few days ago, Mr. Mansur, who is the head of Central Mortgage, told me that it is government policy not to lend money directly in cities with a population of 5,000 or more, for individual house construction. In view of the attitude of the insurance companies it seems to me that such a policy is the height of folly, and I suggest that it should be changed by parliament at once. Therefore surely the second step that is needed, if we want to get a housing program started, is to utilize section 31A of the housing act. After all, that is the reason it was put on the statute books. Surely members do not put 55704-27i
The Address-Mr. Power legislation on the books just to hear themselves talk. I say that our budgetary surplus is such that Canada can well afford to go ahead with such an investment program in housing. And I suggest, too, that if Canada did go ahead with this program, by using the nation's credit, the government could lend money to house builders at interest rates substantially lower than those now prevailing. In this way they would save house builders some hundreds of dollars over the 20-year contract period.
It may be that in connection with housing the provincial and municipal governments are partly at fault. I do not know. However it might be a good thing if the Minister of Resources and Development, before spring is here, got on a plane, as he did when he first took over his portfolio, and visited each provincial capital. Such a trip would enable him to discuss housing with the various provincial and municipal authorities. Perhaps by such a conference some of the red tape and difficulties could be eliminated.
We in the C.C.F. group believe today, as we have believed in the past, that a subsidized low-rental program is the only real solution to our housing problem. But if the government refuses to embark upon such a program, we do call upon it to adopt the three proposals I have just made: First, material priorities for housing construction; second, reduced down payments of only 10 per cent or less and, third, direct financial loans on the balance, where insurance companies refuse to lend. I suggest that we start making use of our building potential. I urge the minister to make a full statement to the house with respect to housing, at the first opportunity.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I propose to make a few observations with respect to the redistribution of seats in the House of Commons, or the readjustment of representation. I am fully aware that there is before the house at the moment a bill standing in the name of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), and that at the last session there was a bill standing in my name, and that both these bills deal with the readjustment of representation in the House of Commons.
This evening I do not propose to do anything more than speak in a broad and general way as to the methods adopted in carrying out the redistribution of representation in the house. Methods of redistribution have been talked about in the house as far back as the earliest days following confederation. In 1903 Sir Wilfrid Laurier, then leader of the government, asked the house to adopt

The Address-Mr. Power a system involving a change from the system which theretofore had been in effect. The old system consisted in the government of the day bringing down a bill to which was attached a schedule, and it was then the duty of the house to indulge in a dog-fight in the house with respect to it, rather than to discuss the matter in committee with a certain amount of acrimony, as has occurred in subsequent years.
Since 1903 suggestions have been made that the method be changed. In 1937 a committee was asked to study methods of redistribution in effect in other countries, and in other parts of the commonwealth. In 1938 the same study was made, and again in 1939. In 1940, as a member of the government of the day, I was instructed by that government to prepare a bill and introduce it to the house, the purpose of which was to set up a commission which would proceed to the preparation of a scheme of redistribution which would afterwards, naturally, be submitted to the house for approval or otherwise. I am fully aware also that, because the cold war had terminated and the real war had begun, that bill was left by the wayside. No attempt in the way of legislation was made since that time, until we reached the last session.
I am fully aware also that neither the bill which is introduced by the government.-and I say that just in passing-nor that which I sponsored at the last session, proposed any change in the method of sharing seats as between provinces. Both of them propose to adhere to the constitutional amendments, as we have them from 1867 to date. I say that because I do not propose to discuss this evening the opportunity or otherwise of endeavouring to amend the constitution in order to prevent the losing of a certain number of seats by any of the provinces.
The principal argument used in the house- and it is a perfectly good alibi: I used it myself at the time of the last redistribution- against setting up a redistribution commission is the time element. It is true that to proceed to obtain a scheme of redistribution from an outside, non-partisan commission would take a considerable period of time. First of all, the house itself or some committee thereof would have to discuss the matter. Secondly, it would be obliged to lay down certain precepts or principles to be adopted by the commission it set up. Then the commission itself would have to make a study of conditions across the country, and finally make a report which, necessarily, would have to be submitted to the house for passage and adoption. That, to me, is not a peremptory reason for neglecting to study methods of redistribution other than that now in force in this country.
[Mr. Fower.l
If the government feels it must have a readjustment during this year, then I suppose it is quite within its rights and its responsibilities to proceed to this readjustment by the most rapid manner possible. After all, no one in the house, except members of the government, knows when the dissolution will take place. The government alone has the right to advise the crown as to when such dissolution should take place. So that it is rather difficult for any of us to cavil at the decision of the government to have what I might call a short-term plan.
What I should like to suggest to the house is that there should be no difficulty, no incongruity in a committee, other than the one being set up to effect redistribution, making a study of other methods which could be put into effect. I suggest that the committee on privileges and elections might meet simultaneously with the committee on redistribution to study other methods which might be more effective, more equitable and more in the interests of the Canadian people as a whole. Such a study need not interfere with the progress of the redistribution bill. I would anticipate that such a study would be improved by the experience which new members would have of the difficulties and turmoil and troubles of the persons who are endeavouring to carry on equitable distribution by the means presently available.
I would rather anticipate that the righteous among us would feel that they were strengthened in their support of a non-parti-sajn scheme of redistribution by what they will see if the committee runs true to form and follows what has occurred in past years. From what will be seen in the committee I anticipate that even those who profit from the manipulation will possibly want to consider some other means of redistribution in the hope that by a sort of tardy repentance they may obtain ultimate forgiveness.
The point I wish to make is that there seems to be no earthly reason, if we hope to achieve a proper redistribution once and for all, a proper scheme of redistribution for the whole country, why a study thereof should be restricted to perhaps the year after a general election. In almost every other year we are apt to be told, "It is too late; we must get ready for the next election; we cannot carry on with a scheme of redistribution for the last election, we must have the new one." It seems to me that if a new method is desired, almost any time is the time to study it.
Now as to the reasons for an alteration in the methods. I venture to say that even members of the government are prepared to admit that the present system is untidy, is

haphazard, is unsatisfactory and, above all, does not carry with it the conviction of the Canadian people that it is fair. It is true that nowadays in our idolatry of material success, in our following of the cult of win at any cost, we have departed in our morals, in our finances, in our politics and, worst of all, in our sports from our former and ancient ethical standards. But even today I am convinced that the public are not prepared to take as an accepted standard anything which even, unjustly or wrongly, they suspect of being the product of manipulation. Stacking the cards and cogging the dice are still not considered and looked upon as gentlemanly and sportsmanlike accomplishments, even in politics.
I would not want in any way to cast aspersions on hon. members who were members of former committees of former parliaments which passed the various redistribution bills, but the suspicion exists in the public mind that those redistributions had for their primary motive political advantage or personal political interests. It seems to me that the time has now come when the members of this house should endeavour to dissipate that suspicion that exists in the minds of the public.
I suggest that that can best be done by providing a new basic and fundamental procedure. Nothing but a new deal, approved of by this House of Commons, can satisfactorily dissipate some of the inequalities presently existing, some of which have sanction of history and tradition, others of which were based on what was considered in those days, and perhaps even in these days, as sound principles. But with all the good will and non-partisanship in the world, I submit that it would be extremely difficult for this house by itself, without the assistance of someone from outside, to endeavour to equalize the inequalities which presently exist. I suggest that the pressures which will come upon us from fair-minded, civic-minded citizens who are imbued with a sense of tradition and the importance of the localities in which they live, will be such that it will be a most difficult burden for the members of the house to bear.
In making our past redistributions we have thought in terms of personalities and parties, the constituency as related to personalities, whereas in a truly democratic state we should be looking at the constituency in the terms of the electors. I have been reading, and I commend it to members of this house who are interested in redistribution, a work entitled "The Canadian House of Commons" by Norman Ward, professor of economics at
The Address-Mr. Power Saskatchewan university. There is a very interesting and instructive chapter on redistribution, and I quote one sentence which he attributes to the late Right Hon. Mr. Mackenzie King and which can be found in 1932-33 Hansard at page 5468, as follows:
Mr. King said:
Anyone reading the Hansard report . . . must realize to how small an extent the redistribution being effected at the moment is based upon the foundational principle of the division of the various constituencies according to the general interest of the country as a whole.
I continue with Mr. Ward:
Although this statement was being applied speci-ficially to the fiasco of 1933, it could be made with equal force concerning even the most peaceful of the eight redistributions which have occurred thus far.
On page 46 Mr. Ward goes on to say:
At one time or another in this contentious history, as we have seen, no less than four principles have been followed: the use of local boundary lines; the adoption of relatively large urban divisions; the establishment of contact divisions; and the equalization of population. But one or more of these principles has always been applied in relation to the wishes of a majority of the House of Commons, and when it has been expedient not to observe a principle, it has been conveniently forgotten.
I suggest that a drastic major operation is needed, not the mere lancing of a boil or two here or there on the body politic; and, moreover, that the longer the operation is deferred the worse will be the disease and the condition of the patient.
Now I should like to suggest to the majority of this house another consideration, that of just what political advantage is derived by the effecting of a redistribution by the party in power. As my friends and associates from Quebec know well, I have never been a white-plumed Sir Galahad constantly seeking the Holy Grail of electoral purity. I look at these matters rather from the standpoint of the hard-boiled politician; and I say to my friends and to myself: what is there to gain by even a manipulated redistribution? I look back at the pages of history within my own recollection and beyond it. I start by studying the very interesting brochure written by MacGregor Dawson entitled "The Gerrymander of 1882" in which Mr. Dawson, after a very earnest and sincere *study of what historically has been considered the worst redistribution we have ever suffered, comes to the conclusion that Sir John Macdonald and his followers gained nothing whatever at the election which followed the redistribution. On the contrary they lost a great many votes in the gerrymandered seats and more than held their own in the seats which had not been gerrymandered.

The Address-Mr. Power
Now I come to 1914, which is within the recollection of a great many of us. In that year the government of Sir Robert Borden effected a redistribution; but those who have observed the political history of that day I think will come to the conclusion that had the House of Commons not extended its term but held an election in 1916, there was more than a good prospect that the opponents of Sir Robert Borden would have come into power. It is quite true that when 1917 came on, with a question which was of vital interest to people all across the country, then questions of redistribution no longer entered into the discussion in any way whatever, and no longer could be counted upon to sway the balance of power from one side to the other.
In 1924 a redistribution was made by the government of the late Mr. King. At that time there were no representatives on the Conservative side from the province of Quebec, so it is to be assumed that had the Liberals in that province wished they could have worked their wicked way. But in 1925 the Liberals were defeated at the polls. Mr. Meighen was returned with 116 seats while the Liberals had 101. If the government remained in power it was due entirely to something else than redistribution. In 1930 the Conservatives came into power on the 1924 distribution.
Following the same line of argument, the Conservatives had a much discussed redistribution committee in 1933. There was bitter controversy in this house over that redistribution. It was alleged to be the most notorious of all the gerrymanders that had taken place. Yet in 1935 the Liberals were returned to power with a very great majority. I do not speak of 1947 because, whatever may have been done by the committee of that year, I do not think anyone will allege that the overwhelming majority the government obtained in 1949 was due to the redistribution.
There is another reason. I have reached the conclusion that nowadays people are not, as the Gilbert and Sullivan play said, all born little Liberals or little Conservatives. There is no longer the same allegiance to party lines. Professor A. R. M. Lower, now of Queen's university, had a very interesting article in the Canadian Historical Review of September, 1946, on what he called "Determinism in politics". In discussing it with him I call it political predestination. He starts with a very amusing dissertation on two well known men then in public life, the Right Hon. Mr. King and the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen. He discusses their physical characteristics and comes to the conclusion, as Shakespeare did, that those who have a lean and hungry look

are apt to be radical whereas those who are more rotund are apt to be conservative. He comes to the conclusion that he was wrong in that case. In comparing Mr. Meighen with Mr. King, his premises do not work out to *their logical conclusion. But he does give some interesting accounts of what he -calls predeterminism arising out of racial reasons, religious reasons and sometimes out of economic reasons.
In speaking of Winnipeg where he lived for some time, and I paraphrase in far cruder language than Professor Lower used, he mentions one constituency of which he knew, in which it would appear that the people who lived in the mansions voted Tory; those who lived in the houses voted Grit; and those who lived in the shacks probably voted C.C.F. If I have the time, the members of the house would be interested, perhaps, in reading of a riding about which he speaks in the following terms:
Group allegiance has decided many an election in Canada; in fact it may have decided most. In the riding known best to the author of this paper, there is a township of Scottish Presbyterians, who always lose their votes, and another of Irish Roman Catholics, who also lose their votes: they both vote Liberal. The solid mass of the riding is north of Ireland. Since confederation, it has never elected anyone but a Conservative. Whatever the issue of the day, personal observation forces the conviction that, as the average elector in that riding goes into the polling booth, he sees rising up between him and his ballot images of William of Orange and the Pope. He accordingly puts an X opposite the Conservative candidate's name, thus winning over again the battle of the Boyne.
May I say to my friends from Quebec also that many times we have won the battle of St. Eustache, and many another time, poor unfortunate Riel has been hanged from the hustings. My contention is that what he calls group allegiance has largely disappeared, and that from the past few elections we would almost come to the conclusion that people do not vote by sections; they do not vote by organizations; they do not vote by race; and they do not vote by religion. Even within families, the call of party loyalty is far less potent than it was. I venture to say that men and women under thirty-five, perhaps even under forty, are no longer influenced by party slogans and party shibboleths.
If hon. members here will agree with that theory, then I suggest to them that it is a waste of time and a waste of our tempers and a waste of our patience to endeavour to hive the Grits, shepherd the Tories or segregate the C.C.F. when few of us, if any, can tell with any certainty just where the habitat of the Grits, the Tories or the C.C.F. is. Under these circumstances the system which we have is not an equitable one. From a

material, political-gain standpoint it does not do any good. I suggest to the government and to this house that we endeavour seriously, by some studies, to arrive at a method which will be more in line with our democratic thought.
I suppose I shall be asked what motives I have for all this agitation. The answer is simply this. I have been here for a long time, and I have been associated with this House of Commons for a still longer time.
I have come to feel all its moods and tenses.
I know its frailties and its greatness. I can even stand, Mr. Speaker, for the pomp and ceremony of it, though I must say that I enjoy the coarse ribaldry that sometimes occurs. In all this time I have learned to admire this House of Commons as an institution, almost to venerate it. I would regret to see it do anything which would lower it in the opinion of the people of Canada, and greatly desire to see it do something which would elevate it in the opinion of the people.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is for me a very great honour and a privilege to be given the opportunity to speak here, particularly since I do so as the member for one of the oldest counties in the province of Quebec, the county of Stanstead. Without further ado, I shall join those of my colleagues who have spoken before me and warmly congratulate the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne (Messrs. George and Gauthier). They have nobly fulfilled their tasks and have depicted their counties from the historical, industrial and economic viewpoints. I think they have done very well and I extend to them my warmest congratulations.
And now, may I be allowed to compare our government to a huge fountain, equipped with taps, the various departments being the guardians of that fountain from which flow so many good things to the advantage of the various sections of the country. Quite naturally, I am tempted to draw nearer to that fountain, and try to show, to the best of my ability, what my county needs most.
May I, first of all, take you to the southern part of my constituency, situated on the frontier of Vermont, where we find three beautiful towns: Stanstead, Rock Island and Beebe. The bilingual population of those towns lives in perfect harmony.
Rock Island is a small village really made up of two municipalities.
Half of the small town of Beebe is located on the American side and the other half on the Canadian side of the frontier.
The Address-Mr. Roberge
We are somewhat privileged in our part of the country since we benefit from three cultures, or rather from three ways of life. First, we have inherited from our forbears a French culture enriched by the Latin culture and civilization. We also greatly benefit from the great business sense of our Englishspeaking citizens. We also enjoy the friendship of our good neighbours to the south. As I was saying a moment ago, the people of these three villages live in perfect harmony.
We have in Rock Island the South Stanstead United Church, members of whose congregation live both in the county of Stanstead and on the American side of the border. We also have two international organizations, the Rotary Club and the Chamber of Commerce, whose members come from both sides of the border as well. Meetings of these two groups take place on Canadian soil, at the Delmonty Hotel in Rock Island; perfect understanding prevails throughout.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to call the government's attention to the state of the granite industry in the town of Beebe. As is well known, granite quarrying is the main industry in Beebe; it employs mostly male labour. There are also a few textile plants where the labour force is mixed but predominantly female.
For some time the granite industry has not been as flourishing as it was in the past and I wish particularly to call the attention of the government to that point. In fact, I have been given rather exact information and data which made me realize that this condition is due to the importing of granite from overseas. Since the transportation costs of this granite are not very high and since our workers are paid higher wages than their counterparts overseas, our granite industry suffers very much from this condition.
One of the oldest companies in the village has laid off almost 75 per cent of its employees, who are mostly householders. I ' ask the government to come to the assistance of the people of this village. However, if the treaties signed at Torquay and Annecy and other similar agreements prevent them from doing so, I wonder whether the Department of Public Works might not, by granting contracts to that company, assist these unfortunate people. I wish to draw the government's attention to this problem and I hope it will lend a sympathetic ear.
Let us now come back to Rock Island, my home town. The situation there is none too

The Address-Mr. Roberge encouraging and it might be even more serious, from the government's point of view. I am referring to the customs office, a matter which has been discussed for many years. Plans were even prepared and then other plans were drawn up later on but the project never got beyond the offices of the architects and engineers. That plan has never materialized and I wish to call the attention of the government to this problem. I have been assured recently, however, that special consideration was being given to this matter. I surely hope so, for tourists coming from the United States and Canadians going to the neighbouring country have to go down a very steep hill before coming to a narrow street where all the stores of that district are concentrated.
In the summer months traffic is very heavy, especially on holidays; one may see over a distance of a mile or a mile and a half a line-up of automobiles that have to wait there in the hot sun after travelling 200, 250 or 300 miles; the nerves of these people are therefore a little on edge, so that when they get to the customs office-I had that experience myself as I was formerly employed there- those people, being very tired, do not want to co-operate in any way. They cannot be blamed. The customs officers have, needless to say, a very complicated task to perform, and if the government wanted to go ahead with this project, the situation would be alleviated and would, I am convinced, strengthen the friendship which the Americans have for us.
When tourists have to go through such a bottleneck, all sorts of rather unpleasant remarks are heard. I am speaking of route 5, which is the main highway between the city of Boston and Quebec; the traffic of four or five American states moves on that road, and you will readily understand that, during the summer months, traffic is rather heavy and the situation becomes intolerable. As there are few warehouses, truckers often have to leave their goods out in the rain; the customs officers then have to work in the rain, and the goods often get spoilt.
I do hope that following the observations which I have just made, the government will see fit to give this problem particular attention.
At the other end of my county, as well as in Stanhope the same condition prevails. For there are no warehouses and the employees have to work practically in the open. Fortunately, I have been told that no later than next year, this problem will be given proper consideration.


(Text):
I now wish to continue in English in relating some of the difficulties which we run across in my county and which I wish to bring to the attention of the government. One of them has been mentioned by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann), and I do not think I should elaborate on it. I may mention, however, that we are also greatly affected by the situation in the textile industry, which is exceedingly gloomy, with people working two and three days a week, and families disappearing overnight by the hundred, so I have been told. The same thing prevails in Coaticook on a smaller scale. These things I am sure will be looked into and I do not need to elaborate any more. I am sure there will be an adjustment in the shortest possible time.
The next thing has to do with the north of the county in Lennoxville, one of the cities in my constituency. There things are just about as normal as they could be. It is a very nice locality and very close to Sherbrooke. I have no complaints about that part of the county at all. I must give a lot of credit to the electors of my county for the way in which they look at this. With all these troubles prevailing they have been very generous to me. They have understood some of the problems that I have tried to explain to them, and they have co-operated a hundred per cent. I wish to congratulate them on bearing with the government and with the country in so far as this unfortunate situation is concerned, which we hope will not last very long. The centre of the county is mostly agricultural. In one section in the central part which is near Massawippi there is an agricultural section which covers about 40 square miles roughly and which has good farms. On the whole things are not too bad, but some of our farmers are complaining on account of the outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease in the west. As I said a few minutes ago, they understand the situation and they understand the problem that is facing the government, but there are some hardships which confront them. For instance, a friend of mine had two or three loads of hay which had been purchased, but which he could not get over the line. Some of the farms just across the border depend on that hay, and that is especially true of last year when we had such prosperous crops. We had a lot of hay to dispose of, and now it cannot be sold.

I did not mention germs. I mean the situation exists, on account of this disease that has broken out in the west. It affects the whole economy of the border from coast to coast, as far as I understand the situation. It prevents our export of hay to the United States. We have a very good market for dairy cattle across the border which was also affected. I feel confident also that if in the near future, after a thorough investigation of the eastern parts, especially in our province, there are no signs of the disease spreading, this embargo will be lifted and things will get back to normal, which will help our farmers quite a lot, and we shall be able to export our hay.
Another problem that we have run into, and which some of our farmers have asked me many times to mention, is the drop in the price of pork and meats of all kinds, and eggs and poultry, and yet they have to pay such enormous prices for their feed. In our part of the country we have beef, pork and poultry. The farmers have to pay $4.10 for a hundred pounds of scratch feed, and eggs are selling for around 38 cents to 42 cents a dozen. Well, they cannot make much headway at those prices. The same thing applies to some of the cattle feed as well. The hon. member for Portneuf (Mr. Gauthier) said this afternoon that some pork has sold as low as 15 cents and 10 cents a pound, and yet the farmers have to pay up to $4.75 for starters. These prevailing prices are rather high when you take into consideration what they get for the produce of the farm. I should like to talk to some of the members of the cabinet and find out the answer. However, I am sure that after discussing the problems things will get back to normal.
I should now like to deal with some general matters, Mr. Speaker. I was in the national revenue service for some time. We ran into a lot of grief. There is one regulation that I should like the government to take into consideration and change it somewhat. It would not amount to very much, just a few dollars. At the present time gifts from abroad, from the United States or from any other country, are allowed in duty free to the value of $5. The sum of $5 for the
The Address-Mr. Roberge average family these days does not mean very much. We know very well that these gifts are occasionally sent to the individual, but mostly they are for the general welfare of the family, man and wife and children. Instead of having the $5 that we have now,
I think that we could raise it to the amount of $15. That would be quite a favourable change and it would avoid the customs officers on the steamship lines or on the border, or anywhere, where these gifts come in through customs ports of all kinds. It would relieve the situation and help out matters quite a lot. Many arguments are caused when people go to claim a parcel at customs which has the value of $5 on it. We know that sometimes the amount of $5 is a little bit off key. If we had a value of $15 in the customs regulations it would benefit our people and it would not do any harm at all as far as revenue is concerned. I would strongly recommend that the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) take this into consideration.
Another item that I should like to draw to the attention of the government has to do with the income tax brackets. We know today, especially in our part of the country where the families are large, sometimes one or two in a family are exceptionally good at school and they want to pursue their studies right up to university or to take special courses of some kind. There is an exemption for children and we have the family allowances up to 16. From 16 to 21 there is a deduction for anyone in a university or a college, but when the individual reaches 21 the exemption is no longer granted. I know of two or three cases where real talents have been lost on account of lack of funds to carry on with their studies. I would suggest that the exemption age for students in universities and schools be raised to 25 years. I think that would just about compensate them and then they could take care of themselves. Two cases have been brought to my attention where the families were quite large and one individual was doing exceptionally well in university but could not take the advanced course. The father may say that he is out of funds, that he has used up all his money, that he has only a little left and cannot afford to spend more. However, through securing loans, and by other methods, he manages to secure enough funds. This is a hardship for the family, and I suggest some measure of relief is required. If the income tax branch would raise the age limit to 25 years, whereby a certificate could be made under regulations prescribed by the minister, it would be beneficial and would help these young men to finish school.

The Address-Mr. Poulin
I believe I shall wait until the budget debate to discuss other matters I have in mind. I do not pretend to be well versed in matters connected with foreign policy. However, in closing may I endorse the remarks of my colleague, the hon. member for Port-neuf (Mr. Gauthier). A number of immigrants have come to our section of the country, some of whom have been first-class, others not quite so satisfactory, and a few who have proved unsatisfactory.
It has been our experience that many of the immigrants would like to sneak across the boundary line to the United States. I have in mind one instance of a gentleman who came from the woods in northern Ontario. He travelled in light clothing and without warm footwear, in sub-zero weather. It happened that he knew one of the immigrants who had settled near the international boundary line. Those people had some difficulty in getting rid of their visitor. He had nowhere else to go and, in the sub-zero weather, they did not wish to turn him out. In the minds of immigrants of that kind-and we see it often in my part of the country-there is only one thought: How can we get across to the United States?i
Let me say, concerning the remarks of the hon. member for Portneuf, that in my part of Canada we are 100 per cent in favour of immigration, but we would confine it to a select group of immigrants who would be prepared to fulfil their contracts, and to conform to our way of living. I believe that I shall leave to the debate on the budget any further remarks I may have to make. (Translation):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in keeping with a very pleasant custom but more particularly out of personal conviction it gives me pleasure to associate myself with most of the previous speakers who have congratulated the mover and seconder (Mr. George and Mr. Gauthier) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
When we read those speeches where everyone boasts about his own district, we find ourselves loving still better this beloved Canada of ours.
Like the rest of Canada, the people of Beauce county were deeply grieved upon learning of the death of our king, especially since he was a humane and understanding king. The people of my constituency have adopted an attitude of respect and submission towards Her Majesty the new Queen.


As long as we are governed by the present system of constitutional royalty, I am confident that our people will always show the greatest respect for the man or woman in whose hands the sceptre rests.
I wish to express to the government, and more particularly to the Prime Minister, my personal gratitude for having chosen a Canadian as governor general. It is universally recognized that the actual holder of the post is a fine man, eminently qualified for this high office. But that is only accidental; the main thing is that it has been finally recognized that a Canadian was capable of occupying this exalted post just as well as a person belonging to another nationality.
Our country having ceased to be, at least in name, a dominion, is gradually becoming conscious of its responsibilities and worth. Let us hope that it will not stop there. There is still a long way to go before it is wholly emancipated and before it achieves the standing of a republic which, to my mind, would be the ideal of statehood.
But until then it will no doubt be possible to walk on, slowly but surely, and to give ourselves along the way, first of all, let us say, a flag which would make our presence known wherever we may foe

and God knows we are in a great many places today-but which would enable us, above all, to give a concrete form to the hopes and aspirations of all those youths who do not know where to look when they want to see the symbol of their country, for which they often generously sacrifice their comfort and sometimes lay down their lives.
And why should our country, once well on the way to independence, not give itself a national anthem?
Among other things, the speech from the throne says this:
Your approval will also be sought for a further Canadian contribution to the Colombo plan.
That, in my humble opinion, is a sound idea and it is well to mention it and to repeat it in this house; it meets with my full approval. For my part, I would be willing to increase it, for example, by any amount that might be deducted from the sums spent for military purposes in Asia. In fact, I am convinced that the way to make friends in that part of the world is not by brilliant feats of arms, by the success of our cannons and our planes but rather by giving aid to satisfy hunger, to create ambition and joy of living and to cause the gratefulness of the stomach if not of the heart.

And now, a few words about the foot-and-mouth disease-the awful fever, as some people call it-which is becoming a national disaster. First of all, I wonder if people are right in blaming the government for its so-called want of care or negligence. There were on the spot experts from both the provincial and federal governments. It is recognized that they took a long time in diagnosing the disease but it must be recognized also that in the case of animals as in the case of human beings it is sometimes impossible to diagnose the disease at the onset. When microbes or virus diseases are involved, the symptoms change very much, precisely because the characteristics of the microbe or virus keep changing and also because the reactions of the diseased animals change so much through successive generations.
At all events, let the experts bear their own responsibilities but let us not be too eager to condemn them, at least until we have proof of their carelessness or of their incompetence.
In this connection I read a few days ago in La Presse of March 11 a piece of news which worried me considerably. The article was entitled "Unanimous approval in Edmonton".
Yesterday evening, the legislature of Alberta approved a motion asking the federal government to take immediate measures in order to abolish the embargo which five Canadian provinces have laid on the import of meat from the west.
Will the federal government consider favorably such a request? Will it take a bias which would neutralize the embargo clamped on meat by the province of Quebec? I would imagine that it is not without due consideration that the provincial government has come to such a decision. I know from the newspapers that the man who is at least partly responsible for that embargo and who is responsible for its enforcement is none other than Dr. Maxime Veilleux, a veterinary doctor of great talent and renown, a graduate from Cornell university, a credit to the province of Quebec and to the county of Beauce in particular. It was indeed in a parish of that beautiful county that he began to practise.
Neither am I forgetting that Mr. Abel Marion, general chairman of the U.C.C. of Quebec, has publicly expressed his thanks to the provincial authorities for their action. This is an extract from a recent statement of his. I am quoting Le Devoir of March 3:
Quebec had to lay the embargo. The chairman of the U.C.C., Mr. Abel Marion, thanks the provincial authorities.
As the only effective remedy known against foot-and-mouth disease is the slaughtering of the stricken animals, the outbreak of this disease in our province would result in a milk shortage for
[DOT] 55704-28J
The Address-Mr. Poulin our towns. The U.C.C. thinks, therefore, that by laying the embargo on shipments of stock from the west of Canada, the provincial government is looking after the best interest of all the people in Quebec.
Such a step might well be criticized in certain quarters. On the other hand, the U.C.C. believes that the provincial department of agriculture had no other means of preventing the infection of our herds and, therefore, the ruin of our breeders. The position taken is courageous and praiseworthy and, once again, it benefits the people of the province at large.
Mr. Marion is a bona fide farmer who has won and, what is more, has kept the confidence of the united farmers of his province. I must say that he always talks sensibly, not only when he praises the government, but when he criticizes it, as he is likely to do at times. Since men like Dr. Maxime Veilleux and Mr. Abel Marion approve the position of the Quebec government, I deem myself justified in asking the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) to refrain from taking any steps that would render void or ineffective the embargo imposed by the government of that province.
I wish to say a few words on a subject which, though it may not be as highly topical as the infection of which I have just spoken, is nevertheless a nightmare for the parties immediately concerned. I mean the sale of pork.
Last Saturday I was visited in my home by a group of farmers from the parish of St. Honore de Beauce. They had brought me a petition which they had circulated in great haste among their friends, the hog producers of the district. In a few hours this request was covered with 165 signatures.
St. Honore is an average agricultural parish in my constituency. The farmers are relatively prosperous because they are hard-working, thrifty, and: because they know how to turn to account the small income afforded by their calling. I repeat that in that one parish, in the space of a few hours, 165 hog producers asked to have their grievances brought to the attention of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) through their representative in Ottawa.
And what do they ask? Briefly this: that in view of the price of feed, the floor price of 26 cents a pound for pork is much too low; that, moreover, the floor price is not maintained in the Quebec market.
Some may refer to provincial autonomy but, for my part, this leaves me cold, providing the farmers get a reasonable price for their products. As a matter of fact, I have in my hand forty-one copies of invoices given me by these good farmers, and I see that in the

The Address-Mr. Poulin weeks of February 25 last and March 3, those farmers were paid at the Legrade, Inc. packing plant, in Quebec city, 20 cents a pound for class A hogs and 19-6 cents for class B-l. Those people were right in asking that a floor price be enforced in Quebec as elsewhere.
1 also received yesterday a letter from another producer in my county, Mr. Gerard Veilleux of Ste. Clothilde de Beauce. He told me in his letter that he sold his hogs and he enclosed a recent bill from which I saw that in that case also Legrade Inc. had paid 20 and 19 cents per pound. If I had the time, I could quote from that letter and I think I could prove, by the figures submitted, that that gentleman lost the sum of $58.61 on the sale of four hogs.
Confronted by those stupendous facts, I went to the extent, yesterday morning, of writing a message to the packing house of the Cooperative Federee, in Quebec, in order to find out what is going on in that establishment. I wrote:
Could you let me know what price was paid for hogs, grades A and B, which reached packing house, February 23, and March 3, 4 and 5?
Soon afterwards, I received a most courteous answer, stating:
Since February 16, we pay for grade A hogs support prices Quebec 25J, grade B 25-10.
Naturally, I looked around for some sound explanation of the whole business; I contacted an official in the department, right here in Ottawa. To my great surprise, he told me a thing I did not know; it appears that throughout Canada neither the merchants nor the packers have to pay the minimum price of 26 cents set by the agricultural prices support board. I must confess that I have wondered whether I had misunderstood the matter and a few hours later, I again turned to the same official who gave me the same answer.
I am asking the Right Hon. Minister of Agriculture to enforce, if possible, the payment of that floor price to producers. I also ask him to raise this price at least to 28 cents a pound, for even at that the farmer would produce at a loss.
I received lately a resolution passed by the U.C.C., a southern Quebec federation, which reads as follows:
February 7, 1952
At a meeting held at St. Joseph de Beauce on February 6, 1952, and which was attended by about 300 farmers representing 35 unions of the U.C.C. of southern Quebec . . .
Thirty-five unions, that's something, for sure.
Resolved that whereas the price of pork has fallen disastrously the meeting registers a strong protest against this situation.
Claims from the agricultural prices support board a minimum price of 28 cents.
